7.2 — Tile Collision, Layers & Sorting

Your cave is already solid. You did not make it solid, and until today you could not have explained why it is solid. That is the uncomfortable part: three components are quietly doing heavy work under your feet, and there is a fourth thing — a set of layers that do not exist yet — that your own code from 6.2 is already gambling on. Today you find out what you inherited, and you fix what you assumed.

The Problem: Collision You Did Not Build ~15 min

In 7.1 you painted a ledge and it held you up. Press Play again and stand on the floor, then select the Collision tilemap and read every component on it. There are three you did not add, and each one is load-bearing:

ComponentWhat it contributesWhat it costs
Tilemap Collider 2D Turns tiles into physics shapes. It builds one small collider per solid tile — the whole cave becomes a few hundred separate shapes. Every one of those shapes is a candidate in every physics query. It works, and it is quietly expensive.
Composite Collider 2D Fuses those separate shapes into one merged outline. The tilemap collider feeds it, and it publishes a single clean polygon. One more component to understand, and one setting that silently decides whether it is used at all.
Rigidbody 2D Unity adds this automatically when a composite appears. It is what lets the merged shape be a body the physics engine owns. Nothing, if you leave it alone. It must stay Static — a floor that moves is a bug in a cave.
Already done for you — do not do it twice. If you follow an older tutorial and add a second Tilemap Collider 2D to Collision, you do not get twice the colliders — you get a floor with duplicated shapes and bizarre edge behaviour you will blame on your movement code. Before you add any component in this unit, read the Inspector first. Here is the exact state of the shipped tilemap: the tilemap collider's Composite Operation is set to Merge (older documentation calls this checkbox Used By Composite), and the rigidbody's Body Type is Static.

So your work this hour is not adding collision. It is three tuning jobs: proving the composite is actually doing its job, giving the whole project the physics layers it has never had, and separating solid from decorative — because right now those two things live under one name.

Socratic: Reading a Component You Did Not Write

  1. The tilemap collider builds a shape per tile. The composite merges them. If the merge setting were switched off, how many physics shapes would the cave have, and what evidence would you look for on screen to detect it?
  2. The rigidbody is Static. What does Static mean about the body's willingness to move, and why is that the correct choice for a cave floor rather than an oversight?
  3. Standing on this floor, your ground check from 6.2 succeeds. So does the raycast care whether it hit one merged polygon or four hundred separate tile shapes?
  4. Seams between tiles are a famous platformer bug — the player snagging on an invisible edge. Which of the three components is the fix for it, and why does merging remove edges that art never showed?
  5. Both the Collision tilemap and a decorative backdrop can be painted from the same tileset. What is the only thing that should distinguish them, and where would you record that difference — on the tiles, or on the tilemap object?
  6. Name one thing that should be solid but is not part of this tilemap (a hint: you have been shot at by it since 3.1). Why must it be its own object rather than a painted tile?
Read Function-Level Examples ~10 min

Read each snippet for what it does in isolation. None of these is from a video game — but all of them are about deciding who is allowed to notice whom.

Example 1 — An airport security lane, deciding what gets scanned:

// The belt only asks the scanner about bags whose tag says
// "checked". Every other bag passes the arch untouched.

Example 2 — A hospital triage desk, filtering by category:

if (triageMask.Contains(patient.category))
    {
        Debug.Log("Seen by this desk.");
    }

Example 3 — A restaurant pass, deciding what is visible to the diner:

plate.sortingOrder = -1;  // garnish sits behind the dish

Example 4 — A one-way valve on a brewery line:

// Wort flows down through the valve and cannot flow back up.
// The valve is not a wall - it is a wall with a direction.

Example 5 — Air traffic control altitude bands (comment only):

// Two aircraft at the same spot are only "conflicting" if they
// share a band. Different bands, no conflict, no matter how close.
Architectural specification: the ground check you already own. In 6.2 you wrote a LayerMask field and passed it into Physics2D.Raycast. Open that script and answer before you touch anything:
  • What is that mask field currently set to in the Inspector? Not what you intended — what is actually ticked in the dropdown.
  • If the mask is set to Default, list every object in the Platformer scene that answers your ground raycast. There is more than one, and one of them can shoot.
  • The mask answers "which layers may I hit". What is the equivalent question for the other side — "which layers may hit me"? Find it in the Physics 2D settings.
  • The tag Ground already exists and is already on the Collision tilemap. If you could fix this with a tag instead of a layer, what would the raycast call look like, and what would it cost you every frame?
  • There is a real difference between a tag and a layer in Unity, and you have been using both since Unit 2 without ever making a layer. State the difference in one sentence each.
Build Lab: Layers That Do Not Exist Yet ~25 min

Step 1 — the discovery. Open Edit → Project Settings → Tags and Layers and read the Layers list. Default, TransparentFX, Ignore Raycast, Water, UI, and a handful of empty slots. That is all. There is no Ground layer in this project. Ground is a tag, and it is on the tilemap — but a tag does nothing for a LayerMask. So the mask you built in 6.2 has been masking whatever the dropdown defaulted to, and your physics queries have been wider than you thought.

Step 2 — layer the whole world. You already created Ground back in 6.2, so your ground check had something to mask against. Open Edit → Project Settings → Tags and Layers, confirm it is still there, and then add the layers the rest of this game needs: Player, Enemy, Projectile and Decoration. Renaming an unused slot is normal and expected.

Then go and assign them, object by object: the Collision tilemap becomes Ground; the Player prefab becomes Player; the enemy and turret prefabs become Enemy; the projectile prefab becomes Projectile; and anything you paint that is only scenery becomes Decoration. A layer set only at runtime on one instance is worthless — assign it on the prefab, so every copy inherits it.

Layer or tag — they are not the same tool, and this project has been confusing them. The Collision tilemap already carries the tag Ground, and that tag is what your CompareTag checks read. But a raycast mask cannot use a tag — it needs a layer. That is exactly the bug you hit in 6.2: the check was asking about a layer that did not exist yet, so the mask defaulted to everything. Tags are for identifying one object; layers are for filtering whole categories in a query. You will use both, for the rest of the year, and mixing them up produces bugs that fail silently.

Step 3 — fix the mask, then try to break it. Point the 6.2 mask at Ground and nothing else. Then test the claim: stand next to an enemy and ask the ground check whether you are grounded. Before your fix, what did it say? After?

Step 4 — the collision matrix. In Project Settings → Physics 2D, find the layer collision matrix — the grid of tick-boxes. Decide, layer pair by layer pair, who collides with whom. Then justify two specific ticks: should Enemy collide with Enemy? Should Projectile collide with Decoration?

Architectural specification: sorting, the other kind of layer.
  • Open Project Settings → Tags and Layers again and read the Sorting Layers list. It already contains Bottom, Player and Top. What is a sorting layer for, and which of the two lists answers "who draws in front"?
  • Which list answers "who is allowed to collide"? Write both answers down side by side, because confusing them costs every beginner exactly one evening.
  • Your backdrop, your ground, your player and your attack swing all need an order. Assign sorting layers to each, and say why the swing effect needs its own layer above Player.
  • Two sprites on the same sorting layer still need an order. What is that second knob called, and where does it live?
  • A pillar the player walks behind — which layer does it go on, and does it need a collider at all?
  • Is a sorting layer a physics object in any way? Can a change to sorting ever stop the player falling through the floor? Prove your answer from the two lists.
Painting decoration onto the solid tilemap is the trap this whole lesson exists to close. A pebble, a vine, a distant rock — all of them look correct painted on Collision, and all of them become rock. Then the thing standing on the pebble is you. There are two defensible fixes and you must choose one and defend it: paint decoration onto the No Collision tilemap (simple, and it can never lie to you), or keep it on a solid tilemap and give that tilemap a Decoration layer your queries exclude (more flexible, more to remember). Pick one. Write down why.
Read the Docs: One-Way Platforms ~15 min

You want a ledge you can jump up through and then stand on. That is not a layer's job and not a sorting layer's job — it is a collider property with a direction. There are three honest ways to build it, and they are not equivalent:

ApproachHow it worksWhat it costsWhen it wins
A separate one-way tilemap with its own Tilemap Collider 2D + Composite Collider 2D + Platform Effector 2D, and Used By Effector ticked on the composite The whole tilemap becomes a membrane you pass upward and stand on downward. A third tilemap to maintain, and the direction applies to every tile on it. When you want many one-way ledges and they all behave the same.
Per-tile effector — Platform Effector 2D plus Used By Effector on the tilemap collider Individual tiles in the existing tilemap gain a direction. It fights the composite merge, and you now have two kinds of tile on one grid. Rarely. Know it exists; do not reach for it first.
A loose object — a plain GameObject with a Box Collider 2D + Platform Effector 2D, placed over a gap in the tiles One platform, one object, zero tilemap surgery. The platform is no longer part of the painted level, so it can drift out of alignment with the grid. When you need exactly one or two, and you need them now.

Whatever you pick, the effector has a Surface Arc and an Offset that decide which direction counts as "up". Predict what happens when the arc is rotated 90°, and then try it on a wall.

Choose, Then Justify

  1. Which of the three approaches did you build, and what in your level made it the right one?
  2. A one-way platform that is one tile thick: what happens to the player who is inside it when the effector is added mid-game? Predict before testing.
  3. If a one-way ledge sits on a layer excluded from the player's mask, does the player still stand on it? Which system decides that — the layer mask or the effector?
  4. A one-way platform is a wall with a direction. Name one other object in this project that would improve if it had a direction (the ladder in 7.3 is a clue).
  5. Your ground raycast fires straight down. Does a one-way platform answer it? What does that mean for the player standing on one and trying to jump?
Bug Hunt: Symptoms With Two Possible Causes ~15 min

Bug Hunt

  1. Your player draws behind a wall. Is that a physics layer problem or a sorting problem? State which list you would open first, and what you would change.
  2. Your ground raycast reports grounded while you stand beside a turret. Which setting is too wide, and which two of the five layers you just made would have prevented it?
  3. Set your enemy prefab to the Ground layer by accident. Your ground check now reports grounded whenever the enemy is under your feet. Explain why that happened using only the words mask and layer — and say what else in the game quietly started colliding differently.
  4. Paint decorative rocks onto the Collision tilemap and walk into one. Which of the two fixes from the trap callout is the cheaper one here, and which is the more flexible one?
  5. Untick Used By Effector (or clear Composite Operation back to None) on the one-way tilemap. Does the player still pass through upward? What did that single setting control?
  6. Your projectile hits the turret that fired it and the turret takes damage from itself. Before you solve it with layers, find out how the projectile leaves the barrel today. Which fix is already half-present in your build — layers, or spawn position?
Tinker ~10 min

Tinker: Depth and Direction

  1. Build a foreground pillar on the Top sorting layer with a solid collider, and walk behind it. What classic game moment did you just build, and why does it need both a sorting layer and a collider?
  2. Turn Composite Operation back to None on the tilemap collider and run along a long floor at speed. Can you feel a difference? Then put it back to Merge — did anything else in the game change, or only the feel?
  3. Add a second Tilemap Collider 2D to Collision and press Play. Describe what the Inspector now shows and what the floor does. Remove it. What rule about inherited components did you just learn the hard way?
  4. Write the one-sentence version of a trade-off you made today, in the shape of a Create PT response: what resource did you spend, and what did you save? (Merging a few hundred shapes into one is a good candidate.)

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Name the three components already on Collision and say what each does
  • Explain what a composite fixes, and name the setting that switches it on
  • Say out loud why Ground being a tag was not enough, and extend the physics layers
  • Explain the difference between a physics layer and a sorting layer, with one use of each
  • Fix your 6.2 ground-check mask and prove the fix with a test
  • Defend your choice of one-way platform approach
  • Commit and push
